about: Physics blocks whose maths is a formula (ND3b): each keeps its id, ports and results, and its maths is the Equation below, with a name that says what happens.

equation.name: Pressure from the weight of a layer

source.text: Turcotte, D. L. and Schubert, G. 2014, Geodynamics, 3rd edn, Cambridge University Press

explain.curious: The deeper you go, the more weight sits on top of you. Ten kilometres of water presses about a thousand times harder than the air.
explain.science: Pressure added by a layer of constant density under constant gravity. Fine for oceans and crusts much thinner than the radius; deep interiors need gravity that falls with depth.

references: Zeng, L., Sasselov, D. D. and Jacobsen, S. B. 2016, ApJ 819, 127: mass-radius relation for rocky planets based on PREM, eq. 2 (inverse eq. 3). doi:10.3847/0004-637X/819/2/127

source.text: Zeng, L., Sasselov, D. D. and Jacobsen, S. B. 2016, ApJ 819, 127

explain.curious: An iron-rich rocky world is smaller than a rock-rich one of the same mass, because iron packs tighter.
explain.science: Fit to two-layer (iron core, silicate mantle) models scaled from Earth's seismic profile (PREM), for rocky planets without water or atmosphere. Agrees with the model curves to about 0.01 R⊕ in its range (1 to 8 M⊕, core mass fraction 0 to 0.4); the inverse gives core mass fraction to about ±0.02.

references: Zeng, L., Sasselov, D. D. and Jacobsen, S. B. 2016, ApJ 819, 127: mass-radius relation for rocky planets based on PREM, eq. 2 (inverse eq. 3). doi:10.3847/0004-637X/819/2/127

equation.name: Share of a rocky world's mass in its core
equation.formula:
x = M / M_e
r = R / R_e
f = (c0 - r / x ^ (1 / c2)) / c1

c0.name: radius at no core, Earth radii per Earth mass^(1/3.7)

f.name: share of the mass in the core

source.text: Zeng, L., Sasselov, D. D. and Jacobsen, S. B. 2016, ApJ 819, 127

explain.curious: Weigh a rocky world and measure it, and you can tell roughly how much of it is an iron core.
explain.science: The Zeng et al. 2016 relation inverted. Outside 0 to 0.4 the answer means the world is not a dry iron and rock planet (too fluffy: water or gas; too dense: more iron than the fit covers).

references: Zeng, L. and Jacobsen, S. B. 2017, ApJ 837, 164: a simple analytical model for rocky planet interiors (core radius fraction about the square root of core mass fraction). doi:10.3847/1538-4357/aa6218

equation.name: How oxidised a young mantle is
equation.formula:
fem = max(fe - fc * f, 0)
n = max(fem / mfe - c / mc, 0)
ns = max(1 - f - n * mfeo, 0) / ms
x = if n + ns <= 0 then 1 else n / (n + ns)
core = 2 * log10(max(g * x, x0) / xm)
d = clamp(core + s, -8, 6)

f.name: the core's share of the rock and metal

c.name: carbon free to smelt iron oxide, share of the rock and metal

mfeo.name: molar mass of iron oxide, FeO

fe.name: iron's share of the rock and metal

xm.name: iron's mole fraction in the metal

ms.name: mean molar mass of the other oxides

x0.name: the least FeO a mantle keeps

d.name: the mantle's oxygen fugacity against iron-wüstite, log10 units, at the magma ocean's surface

core.name: the same at core formation, where metal and rock last met

source.text: Wade, J. and Wood, B. J. 2005, EPSL 236, 78
source.where: the iron-wüstite equilibrium between core metal and mantle silicate

explain.curious: How oxidised a planet's rock is decides what its volcanoes breathe out. A world that kept most of its iron as metal in a big core has a reduced mantle that gives off hydrogen and carbon monoxide; one whose iron rusted into the rock gives off water and carbon dioxide.
explain.science: Iron the core did not take stays in the mantle as FeO; its mole fraction against iron's in the metal sets ΔIW = 2 log10(γ x_FeO / x_Fe) at core formation (Wade and Wood 2005). Water has already oxidised some metal (a smaller core), and free carbon smelts FeO back to metal first. A deep magma ocean then oxidises itself, ferrous iron turning to ferric under pressure (Armstrong et al. 2019), which lifts the surface value; one shift for every world (fudge register). Earth comes out near IW-2.2 at core formation and IW+0.5 at its magma ocean's surface (Sossi et al. 2020), Mars about IW+1.2.

references: Stacey, F. D. and Davis, P. M. 2008, Physics of the Earth, 4th edn, Cambridge University Press: the moment of inertia of a layered Earth, C/MR² = 0.3307 measured against 0.4 for a uniform sphere. doi:10.1017/CBO9780511812910
atoms.shown: C = 2/5 [q x² + (1 − q)(1 − x⁵)/(1 − x³)],  x = r_core / R

equation.name: How much of a rocky world's mass sits in the middle
equation.formula:
x = if R <= 0 then 1 else max(rc / R, 0)
C = if x >= 1 then 2 / 5 else 2 / 5 * (clamp(q, 0, 1) * x ^ 2 + (1 - clamp(q, 0, 1)) * (1 - x ^ 5) / (1 - x ^ 3))

source.text: Stacey, F. D. and Davis, P. M. 2008, Physics of the Earth, 4th edn
source.where: the moment of inertia of a layered planet

explain.curious: A uniform ball has a moment of inertia factor of 0.4. Gather mass into a heavy iron core and it falls: Earth's is 0.33, the Moon's, with almost no core, 0.39. Spinning worlds with a low factor bulge less at the equator.
explain.science: A core of mass share q and radius ratio x inside a uniform mantle: I = 2/5 q M r_c² + 2/5 (1 − q) M R² (1 − x⁵)/(1 − x³). Self-compression is left out, so a large rocky world comes out a few per cent above its measured value (Earth 0.35 against 0.3307).

params.description: share of the heavy elements gathered into a small core; the rest mixes through the envelope (a dilute core, Wahl et al. 2017)

references: Hubbard, W. B. 1984, Planetary Interiors, Van Nostrand Reinhold: the n = 1 polytrope for a giant planet, density ρ = ρc sin(πr/R)/(πr/R), whose moment of inertia factor is 2/3 − 4/π² ≈ 0.261

Wahl, S. M. et al. 2017, Geophysical Research Letters 44, 4649: Juno's gravity field asks for a dilute core, Jupiter's heavy elements spread through about half its radius rather than gathered in the middle. doi:10.1002/2017GL073160

equation.name: How much of a giant's mass sits in the middle

z.name: heavy elements' share of the mass

f.name: share of the heavy elements in a small core

explain.curious: A gas giant squeezes its own gas, so it is far denser in the middle than at the top, like a ball of hydrogen pressed by its own weight. That gives Jupiter a factor near 0.25 and Saturn, with more of its mass in a heavy core, near 0.21.
explain.science: Hydrogen and helium under a giant's pressure behave close to an n = 1 polytrope (pressure as density squared), whose density falls as sin(πr/R)/(πr/R) and whose C is exactly 2/3 − 4/π² ≈ 0.261. The heavy elements gathered in a small central core add almost nothing to I, so that share of the mass is taken out; the rest mixes through the envelope (Juno: a dilute core).
